1. What is Deep Learning (vs normal ML)?

Machine Learning (ML): You design features + choose an algorithm.

Example: For house price prediction, you manually create features:
price_per_sqft, distance_to_city_center, no_of_bedrooms, etc.
Then use Linear Regression / Random Forest / SVM.

Deep Learning (DL): The model learns features itself from raw data.

For images: raw pixels → CNN automatically learns edges, shapes, objects.

For text: raw words / tokens → Transformer learns syntactic + semantic patterns.

So:

ML = feature engineering + simple model
DL = big neural network that does both feature learning + prediction

“Deep” means many layers stacked together.

3. Why stacking many layers works (Representation learning)

A deep network builds hierarchical representations:

Layer 1: very low-level patterns

For images: edges, corners

For text: simple word-level patterns

Layer 2–3: more complex patterns

For images: shapes, textures

For text: phrases, grammar

Layer 10+: high-level concepts

For images: faces, cars, objects

For text: meaning, intent, sentiment

Step 3: Backpropagation

To compute gradients efficiently, we use Backpropagation:

Forward pass:
Input → network → output → compute loss.

Backward pass:
Using chain rule of calculus, compute gradients layer by layer from output back to input.
This uses the computational graph.

Key idea:

Each operation (add, multiply, activation) knows how to compute:

output from input

gradient of loss w.r.t. its inputs (given gradient of loss w.r.t. its output)

Frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow automate this (autograd).

5. Optimization Algorithms

Basic Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD):

Instead of using all data each step (too slow), we use mini-batches (like 32, 64 samples).

Noisy but much faster and often better generalization.

Improvements:

Momentum:
Keep an exponential moving average of past gradients; helps escape small local minima and speeds up along ravines.

RMSProp:
Adapt learning rate per parameter based on magnitude of recent gradients.

Adam = Adaptive Moment Estimation:
Combines Momentum + RMSProp. Very widely used.

In practice:

Start with Adam, learning rate like 1e-3 or 3e-4, then tune.

6. Overfitting & Regularization

Deep networks have huge capacity → they can overfit training data.

Signs of overfitting:

Training loss ↓↓ (very small)

Validation loss starts increasing

Accuracy on training >> accuracy on validation

Encourages smaller weights → smoother functions.

Dropout
During training, randomly drop some neurons (set output to 0) with a certain probability (like 0.5).
At test time, use full network but scale weights.
This forces network to not depend on any single neuron → more robust.

Data Augmentation (especially for images)
Random flips, rotations, crops, color jitter, etc.
Makes the model invariant to such transformations.

Early Stopping
Monitor validation loss, stop training when it stops improving.

Batch Normalization
Normalize activations within each mini-batch (mean 0, variance 1), then learn scaling and shift.
Helps stabilize training, allows higher learning rates.

7. Major Deep Learning Architectures
7.1 Fully Connected Networks (MLP)

General structure: Dense layer → activation → Dense → activation…

Good for:

Tabular data

Simple tasks where input dimension isn’t huge

Limitations:

Does not use spatial/temporal structure of data (all features treated similarly).

Too many parameters for high-dimensional inputs like big images.

7.2 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) – for images

Key ideas:

Local Receptive Field:
A neuron in a conv layer looks at a small patch (e.g., 3×3) instead of the entire input.

Weight Sharing:
Same filter (kernel) is applied across the whole image.
→ Greatly reduces number of parameters.

Feature Maps:
Each filter learns some pattern: edge, texture, etc.

Typical pipeline:

Conv → ReLU → Pooling → Conv → ReLU → Pooling → ... → Fully Connected → Output

Pooling (max/avg pooling):
Reduces spatial size, makes network more robust to small translations.

Used for:

Image classification

Object detection

Segmentation

Many computer vision tasks

7.3 RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs – for sequences

Problem: Standard networks assume fixed-size input; sequences (text, time series, audio) have variable length and order matters.

LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) and GRU:

Special RNN cells with gates (input, forget, output) to control information flow.

Better at learning long-range dependencies.

Still, they are sequential (hard to parallelize) and struggle with very long contexts.

7.4 Attention and Transformers – modern NLP & beyond

Transformers solve RNN limitations using self-attention.

Self-Attention:

Each token can directly look at all other tokens.

Computes a weighted sum of other token representations based on attention scores.

High-level:

Input tokens → embed → add positional encoding →
go through multiple Transformer layers:

Multi-head self-attention

Feed-forward network

Residual connections + LayerNorm

Advantages:

Parallelizable across tokens (unlike RNNs).

Captures long-range dependencies efficiently.

Scales very well with data and compute → basis of large language models (like GPT, Gemini, etc.).

Transformers are now used for:

Text (translation, summarization, chatbots)

Images (Vision Transformers)

Audio, time series, multimodal tasks.

8. Full Training Pipeline (End-to-End)

Concrete steps you follow in real projects:

Define the problem

Type: classification, regression, detection, etc.

Data format: tabular, image, text, audio, sequence.

Prepare data

Clean + handle missing values

Train / validation / test split

Normalize / standardize features

Data augmentation (if relevant)

Choose model architecture

MLP, CNN, RNN/LSTM, Transformer, or hybrid.

Decide depth, width, activation functions.

Choose loss + metrics

Loss: cross-entropy, MSE, etc.

Metrics: accuracy, F1-score, precision/recall, AUC, etc.

Choose optimizer + hyperparameters

Optimizer: Adam / SGD-Momentum

LR, batch size, epochs, regularization, etc.

Train

Loop over epochs:

For each batch: forward → loss → backward → optimizer step.

Track training and validation loss/metrics.

Evaluate

On test set (never used during training/validation).

Check for overfitting, underfitting.

Iterate + Improve

Tune hyperparameters

Better architecture

More data / augmentation

Regularization techniques

9. How to go deeper from here

Since you’re already an AI/ML student, a good path would be:

Mathematical foundations

Linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, SVD)

Calculus (derivatives, chain rule, gradients)

Probability & statistics

Hands-on with a framework

Pick PyTorch or TensorFlow/Keras.

Implement:

MLP on MNIST

CNN on CIFAR-10

LSTM / GRU on a text dataset

Small Transformer for text classification

Read some classic papers (with code)

LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet (vision)

LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber)

“Attention is All You Need” (Transformers)

Do small but complete projects

Image classifier

Sentiment analysis

Time-series prediction (stock, weather, etc.)

Something related to your own interests (healthcare, recommender systems, etc.)
